items.content_excerpt: $POET – The photonics revolution is no longer just a future promise. NVIDIA has confirmed that its CPO optical engines are already entering production, with SPIL planning a massive 15x capacity expansion by mid-2027. Meanwhile, POET is scaling its own optical engine manufacturing through NationGate and Globetronics, expects Q4 shipments to exceed the first nine months of 2026 combined, and has seven customers targeting production in 2027. The timing is fascinating. NVIDIA is demonstrating that optical connectivity is becoming essential to AI infrastructure, while POET is positioning itself to participate in this rapidly expanding market. To be clear, a direct POET–NVIDIA supply relationship has not been confirmed der. But the bigger picture is compelling: The market is moving toward photonics, and POET is preparing for scale. 2027 will be a defining year. $POET $NVDA $COHR $LITE Bullish on the technology. items.title: A series of widespread technology outages disrupted major businesses and government agencies over four consecutive business days, affecting
items.content_excerpt: A series of widespread technology outages disrupted major businesses and government agencies over four consecutive business days, affecting Microsoft Outlook, FAA flight operations, JPMorgan Chase transactions, United Airlines departures, the NSA and Apple services. Officials have ruled out cyberattacks or coordinated nation-state activity, attributing the incidents to routine maintenance, software bugs, hardware failures and internal updates. Microsoft’s outage stemmed from an undetected bug dating back to July, while the FAA cited a router upgrade in Arkansas that overwhelmed its telecommunications network. JPMorgan blamed a software bug in its on-premise systems, and Apple attributed its disruptions to an internal update. Security experts warn that AI is accelerating vulnerability discovery and increasing pressure on IT teams to patch systems, while emphasizing the need for stronger digital infrastructure and operational backup plans. $MSFT $AAPL $JPM $UAL

items.title: $PLTR $150 PT in the next few weeks? Not out of the question—but technical confirmation matters. Looking for a breakout above recent resista
items.content_excerpt: $PLTR $150 PT in the next few weeks? Not out of the question—but technical confirmation matters. Looking for a breakout above recent resistance on 1.5x+ average volume, a close above resistance (not an intraday wick), and a successful retest with buyers defending former resistance as support. 21-EMA trending higher, higher highs/higher lows, RSI 60–75, and relative strength vs. $QQQ and AI/software peers would strengthen the setup. Breakout → hold → retest → higher low → continuation. No chasing a vertical spike. A failed breakout, loss of the breakout zone, and breakdown below the 21-EMA on expanding volume invalidates the momentum thesis. $150 is the target. Price action must earn it.

items.content_excerpt: $DIA $DJT $VTI $VTI $SPY Called it, Duffy is a liar, they know it was an attack. "If it looks like a DDoS attack" There is a reason the word DDoS rarely appears in early statements. A “technical issue” is a maintenance problem. An “attack” is a disclosure event: regulators, investors and customers all ask how it got through. Every incentive points to the first label, whether or not anyone acts on it. DDoS, distributed denial of service, is a leading threat to the availability of any publicly accessible online service. Every bank, airline and cloud provider runs hundreds or thousands of services, and each is a potential target. A DDoS attack is the cheapest, most repeatable way for an adversary to buy that hour. For a bank, it means frozen payments, regulatory notifications and customers wondering where else to keep their money. Every executive should be asking one question this week: if someone tried, would ours hold? https://fortune.com/2026/11/17/microsoft-faa-bank-outages-ddos-attack-boards-mazebolt-matthew-andriani/

items.title: $FCEL How does Sky Data centers pair both sofc and mcfc in a data center? "1. The Facility Microgrid (Outside): MCFC + R-SOFC In their
items.content_excerpt: $FCEL How does Sky Data centers pair both sofc and mcfc in a data center? "1. The Facility Microgrid (Outside): MCFC + R-SOFC In their core commercial design (The Sky Energy Stack), they pair two high-temperature technologies outdoors in a charge/discharge loop so the servers are never exposed to raw fuel or grid fluctuations: • Step 1 — Continuous Generation (MCFC): Natural gas feeds outdoor Molten Carbonate Fuel Cells (supplied by FuelCell Energy). Instead of powering the servers directly, these units run steadily to charge an electrochemical energy storage pool. • Step 2 — Long-Duration Storage & Discharge (R-SOFC): That energy is stored in Reversible Solid Oxide Fuel Cells (using Noon Energy's carbon-oxygen battery chemistry, which holds over 100 hours of charge). When the data center needs power, the R-SOFC runs in reverse ("discharge mode") to feed a steady DC bus."

items.title: $FCEL What are the challenges of using PEM tech inside a rack? part 2 "• Heat and moisture management: PEM fuel cells are roughly 50%–6
items.content_excerpt: $FCEL What are the challenges of using PEM tech inside a rack? part 2 "• Heat and moisture management: PEM fuel cells are roughly 50%–60% thermally efficient, meaning nearly half the energy becomes waste heat that the data center cooling system must remove. They also produce liquid water and humid exhaust, which must be drained safely without risking condensation or leaks near live servers. • Fuel cost and logistics: Green hydrogen remains expensive and difficult to deliver or store at scale compared to utility grid power or diesel. Piping hydrogen to dozens or hundreds of individual racks also adds complex plumbing and potential failure points. • Maintenance disruption: Servicing a stack, replacing filters, or troubleshooting a fuel cell inside an active IT aisle is harder and more disruptive than maintaining centralized power equipment in a dedicated mechanical room or yard."

items.title: $FCEL What are the challenges of using PEM tech inside a rack? part 1 "• Hydrogen safety inside white space: Piping pressurized hydroge
items.content_excerpt: $FCEL What are the challenges of using PEM tech inside a rack? part 1 "• Hydrogen safety inside white space: Piping pressurized hydrogen directly into server aisles triggers strict fire codes, ventilation rules, and leak-detection requirements. Because hydrogen has a wide flammability range and rises rapidly, bringing it indoors near high-heat IT gear creates far higher risk and permitting friction than keeping fuel outside. • Lost rack density: Every U of rack space taken by a fuel cell stack, humidifier, air blower, and power electronics is space taken away from revenue-generating servers. In modern high-density or AI racks, operators usually want power generation outside the rack to maximize compute per square foot."

items.title: $FCEL "1. Why They Aren't Testing MCFC (They Already Know It Works) • Mature Commercial Track Record: FuelCell Energy's MCFC sy
items.content_excerpt: $FCEL "1. Why They Aren't Testing MCFC (They Already Know It Works) • Mature Commercial Track Record: FuelCell Energy's MCFC systems already have decades of field data and millions of megawatt-hours generated across utility microgrids, wastewater treatment plants, and industrial facilities. FuelCell Energy packages them in 1.25 MW to 12.5 MW outdoor blocks that connect via standard electrical switchgear." "2. Why They Are Testing PEM (Proving a New In-Rack Architecture) Sky Data Centers' Santa Rosa testbed isn't testing whether PEM works in general; it is testing putting fuel cells directly inside the server row on an 800V DC bus—something that has never been done commercially at scale:"

items.content_excerpt: $SLS $CAPR Good morning, $SLS and $CAPR I'm a shareholder in both SELLAS Life Sciences and Capricor Therapeutics. CAPR has an important FDA decision coming up on November 22. Beren Therapeutics just received FDA approval despite the failure of its initial randomized trial, following a Major Amendment that extended its PDUFA date by 3 months. CAPR's situation is actually different and potentially more encouraging. Its Phase 3 HOPE-3 trial successfully met its primary endpoint with statistical significance. Although one key secondary endpoint did not reach statistical significance, the results were still encouraging, with additional supportive findings across other secondary and exploratory measures. On top of that, CAPR has compelling long-term open-label extension (OLE) data showing sustained clinical benefits, including encouraging cardiac outcomes. Of course, every FDA decision is different, but I find this comparison particularly interesting. Not a finiancial advice

items.title: $CAPR By golly I think I got something here! More juice. Lol Tingting Zhou’s AdCom remarks have been read as making SAP 1.1 the only “prespe
items.content_excerpt: $CAPR By golly I think I got something here! More juice. Lol Tingting Zhou’s AdCom remarks have been read as making SAP 1.1 the only “prespecified” plan. That reverses the sequence. CAPRs position, SAP 3.0 was the final locked plan, finalized and signed before unblinding. Under standard rules, the plan in force immediately prior to unblinding is the governing pre specified analysis. Any departure from it is post hoc. By treating the early, unsigned SAP 1.1 draft as the benchmark and labeling later versions post hoc, FDA inverted that order! The non significant results under SAP 1.1 therefore become the true post hoc analyses because they require discarding the locked plan SAP 3.0, under which the primary endpoint was significant. John Scott’s clarification supports this! When the FDA said “post hoc,” it referred to choices that differed from SAP 3.0. Changing the efficacy result by moving away from the final locked plan makes the SAP 1.1 analyses the post hoc ones, not the reverse.

items.title: $CAPR Thinking about SAP1.1 differently. Dr. John Scott, Director of the Division of Biostatistics at FDAs CBER, explained that when the FDA
items.content_excerpt: $CAPR Thinking about SAP1.1 differently. Dr. John Scott, Director of the Division of Biostatistics at FDAs CBER, explained that when the FDA used the term “post hoc” in presentations, they specifically meant analytic choices made in the clinical study report that differed from SAP version 3.0. Yes, the version finalized right before the data were unblinded. This can be argued that SAP 3.0 should be treated as the governing pre specified plan. The FDAs own review found PUL 2.0 stat sig under SAP 3.0, that favored Deramiocel, and that mid level PUL domain, elbow function, which is important for independence showed stat sig across SAP versions. They also point to the gold standard that shows benefits, cardiac MRI data, which measures fibrosis in the heart muscle and has shown favorable results. Dr. McDonald’s letter and Dr. John Scott, the FDA statistician’s definition, are part of the argument that the governing plan was SAP 3.0 and that the overall evidence supports the drug.

The steep selloff has intensified criticism of management over production-ramp targets and delayed projects, alongside bullish arguments about data-center demand and high short interest.

messages.body: $FCEL How does Sky Data centers pair both sofc and mcfc in a data center? "1. The Facility Microgrid (Outside): MCFC + R-SOFC In their core commercial design (The Sky Energy Stack), they pair two high-temperature technologies outdoors in a charge/discharge loop so the servers are never exposed to raw fuel or grid fluctuations: • Step 1 — Continuous Generation (MCFC): Natural gas feeds outdoor Molten Carbonate Fuel Cells (supplied by FuelCell Energy). Instead of powering the servers directly, these units run steadily to charge an electrochemical energy storage pool. • Step 2 — Long-Duration Storage & Discharge (R-SOFC): That energy is stored in Reversible Solid Oxide Fuel Cells (using Noon Energy's carbon-oxygen battery chemistry, which holds over 100 hours of charge). When the data center needs power, the R-SOFC runs in reverse ("discharge mode") to feed a steady DC bus."

$FCEL What are the challenges of using PEM tech inside a rack? part 2 "• Heat and moisture management: PEM fuel cells are roughly 50%–60% thermally efficient, meaning nearly half the energy becomes waste heat that the data center cooling system must remove. They also produce liquid water and humid exhaust, which must be drained safely without risking condensation or leaks near live servers. • Fuel cost and logistics: Green hydrogen remains expensive and difficult to deliver or store at scale compared to utility grid power or diesel. Piping hydrogen to dozens or hundreds of individual racks also adds complex plumbing and potential failure points. • Maintenance disruption: Servicing a stack, replacing filters, or troubleshooting a fuel cell inside an active IT aisle is harder and more disruptive than maintaining centralized power equipment in a dedicated mechanical room or yard."

$FCEL What are the challenges of using PEM tech inside a rack? part 1 "• Hydrogen safety inside white space: Piping pressurized hydrogen directly into server aisles triggers strict fire codes, ventilation rules, and leak-detection requirements. Because hydrogen has a wide flammability range and rises rapidly, bringing it indoors near high-heat IT gear creates far higher risk and permitting friction than keeping fuel outside. • Lost rack density: Every U of rack space taken by a fuel cell stack, humidifier, air blower, and power electronics is space taken away from revenue-generating servers. In modern high-density or AI racks, operators usually want power generation outside the rack to maximize compute per square foot."

$FCEL "1. Why They Aren't Testing MCFC (They Already Know It Works) • Mature Commercial Track Record: FuelCell Energy's MCFC systems already have decades of field data and millions of megawatt-hours generated across utility microgrids, wastewater treatment plants, and industrial facilities. FuelCell Energy packages them in 1.25 MW to 12.5 MW outdoor blocks that connect via standard electrical switchgear." "2. Why They Are Testing PEM (Proving a New In-Rack Architecture) Sky Data Centers' Santa Rosa testbed isn't testing whether PEM works in general; it is testing putting fuel cells directly inside the server row on an 800V DC bus—something that has never been done commercially at scale:"

$FCEL Sky Data Centers are new to data centers and have not deployed any as of yet. They are very ambitious with their projected growth of 970mz. "Yes—you hit on the exact reasoning behind their strategy. Sky Data Centers is an early-stage developer with zero large-scale commercial campuses operating yet, and their testing approach separates proven utility-scale generation (MCFC/SOFC) from unproven in-rack power architecture (PEM)."

$FCEL Why is Sky Data Centers Honduras project slated for mcfc instead of sofc? "The Puerto Cortés, Honduras project is slated for FuelCell Energy's Molten Carbonate Fuel Cells (MCFC) rather than Bloom Energy's Solid Oxide Fuel Cells (SOFC) primarily because of integrated absorption cooling in a tropical climate, LNG fuel compatibility, and utility-scale baseload modularity.
